subject: korean
title: A claim about the whole class
goal: Use the self-introductions as evidence to decide whether a sentence about everybody is true, see how many exceptions break it, and write a sentence that fits the evidence.
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to say what you like and dislike. Here you test someone else's claim against four short introductions and repair it.
material:
Your class has a chat group. The class has four students. Each wrote a short self-introduction about food. Then 수진 wrote a sentence about the class.

민호: 저는 김치를 좋아해요. 매일 먹어요.
에밀리: 저는 김치를 안 좋아해요. 불고기를 좋아해요.
지아: 저는 김치를 좋아해요. 그런데 매운 김치는 못 먹어요.
토마스: 저는 김치를 좋아해요. 지난주에 처음 먹었어요.

수진: 우리 반 네 명은 모두 김치를 좋아해요.

(모두 = all.)

steps.prompt: 수진 claims that ALL four classmates like kimchi. Which classmate's sentence shows that her claim is not true?

options.reveals: Eating it every day supports the claim; it cannot show that someone dislikes kimchi.
Look at the whole introduction: 지아 also says she likes kimchi. She cannot eat the spicy kind, which is not the same as disliking kimchi.
Eating it for the first time last week says nothing about whether he likes it.

steps.explain: Only 에밀리 answers 'Do you like kimchi?' with no. A claim about everybody is broken by a single person who disagrees. The other sentences are about how much, how spicy or when, not about liking.
hints: For each classmate, decide whether the sentence tells you if he or she likes kimchi.
Keep only the sentences that answer 'Does this person like kimchi?' directly, and compare them with 수진's sentence.

steps.prompt: 수진's sentence says 모두 (all). How many of the four classmates would have to disagree for her sentence to be false?

options.reveals: Two is more than needed. 'All' makes a promise about each single person.
Three is more than needed. 'All' makes a promise about each single person.
Four is far more than needed. 'All like it' already fails as soon as one person does not.

steps.explain: 'All' promises something about every single person, so one exception is enough to break it. A sentence such as '대부분' (most) can survive a few exceptions.
hints: Imagine the class has 100 students. How many people who dislike kimchi would you need to find?
'All of them like it' is true only if nobody is left out. Count how many exceptions break that.

steps.prompt: Write ONE polite Korean sentence about kimchi and the four classmates that is true for the four introductions.

checks.label: is about kimchi (김치)
polite ending (-요 / -습니다)
limits the claim truthfully (most, three people, naming 에밀리 as the exception ...)
does not say that nobody likes kimchi
does not give a wrong count or a wrong exception

selfAssess: Is my sentence true for ALL four introductions, including 에밀리's?
Did I avoid 'all' unless I named the exception?

modelAnswers.text: 네 명 중에 세 명이 김치를 좋아해요.

badAnswers.text: 우리 반 친구들은 모두 김치를 좋아해요.
badAnswers.why: Repeats the claim that 에밀리's sentence breaks.
Overcorrects: three classmates do like kimchi.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is really true for the four introductions and sounds natural.
hints: Decide first how many of the four like kimchi, then write a sentence that is true for exactly that group.
Check your sentence against 에밀리's introduction before you finish.

rubric.full: Finds the sentence that contradicts the claim and says one exception is enough
rubric.partial: Finds the contradiction but thinks several exceptions are needed
rubric.none: Picks a sentence that is not about liking kimchi

rubric.full: Writes a true sentence that names the exception or uses 'most'
rubric.partial: Hedged but not true for all four, or no clear Korean sentence
rubric.none: Repeats 'all' or says nobody likes it

alternatives: '지아 is the exception' is not supported: she says she likes kimchi, only not the spicy kind.
A sentence that keeps 모두 but names the exception ('에밀리 씨 빼고 모두 ...') is also correct.
hardCases: Whether '매일 먹어요' proves liking (it strongly suggests it, but the task does not rely on it).
Learners may write 'Most' in English; the Korean ending check will say it is not a Korean sentence.

cautions.language: Beginner Korean only (해요체, basic particles, numbers up to the thousands). English glosses are given for the few harder words.
cautions.culture: Introductions about food are personal; the task treats them only as short texts to check a claim against.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or sound. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Choice of how many exceptions break 'all'
Kimchi, polite ending, a limited claim and no 'nobody' in the written sentence
human: Whether the written sentence is true and natural

subject: korean
title: Does the note match the chat?
goal: Compare a written summary with the original chat, find the lines that changed a detail, say what kind of detail changed, and write a corrected summary.
thinking: Checking a summary against its source
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read times aloud. Here you must check each detail of a retold plan against what was really said.
prerequisites: Knows Korean time words (두 시, 아홉 시)
material:
민수 and 지나 plan Saturday by chat. Then 지나 writes a note to her mother.

민수: 지나 씨, 토요일 오후 두 시에 학교 앞에서 만나요.
민수: 영화는 세 시 반에 시작해요. 영화를 보고 저녁을 먹어요.
민수: 저녁을 먹고 아홉 시에 집에 가요.
지나: 네, 좋아요!

(앞 = in front of. 집에 가요 = go home.)

steps.prompt: 지나 writes a note to her mother. Some lines do not match the chat. Pick one line of the note that does not match the chat.
lines: 엄마, 저 토요일에 민수 씨를 만나요.
오후 두 시에 영화관 앞에서 만나요.
steps.explain: Two lines do not match the chat. Line 2 says they meet in front of the cinema, but 민수 wrote 학교 앞 (in front of the school). Line 5 says 여덟 시 (8 o'clock), but 민수 wrote 아홉 시 (9 o'clock). Lines 1, 3 and 4 match.
hints: Go through the note line by line and find the same detail in the chat: who, which day, where, what time.
For each line, say whether the chat gives a place or a time for it, and compare the words one by one.

steps.prompt: The wrong lines of the note differ from the chat in two different ways. Which pair is it?

options.text: A wrong day and a wrong place
options.reveals: The day (토요일) is the same in the chat and in the note.

options.text: A wrong person and a wrong day
options.reveals: The person (민수) and the day (토요일) are the same in the chat and in the note.

options.text: A wrong place and a wrong time
A wrong time and a wrong person
options.reveals: The person (민수) is the same in the chat and in the note.

steps.explain: The note changes where they meet (영화관 instead of 학교) and when they go home (여덟 시 instead of 아홉 시). Who and which day are right.
hints: Sort the details of the plan into groups: who, which day, where, what time.
Which two groups contain the details that changed between the chat and the note?

steps.prompt: Write the note to the mother again in correct polite Korean (2 or 3 short sentences). Use the chat to give the meeting place, the meeting time and the time she goes home.

checks.label: meeting place: in front of the school
meeting time: two o'clock, tied to the meeting
going home: nine o'clock, tied to going home
does not keep the wrong details
polite ending

selfAssess: Does every place and time in my note match the chat?
Would my mother know where and when to expect me?

modelAnswers.text: 엄마, 저 토요일 두 시에 학교 앞에서 민수 씨를 만나요. 영화를 보고 저녁을 먹어요. 아홉 시에 집에 가요.
엄마, 토요일 오후 2시에 학교 앞에서 친구를 만나요. 영화랑 저녁을 먹고 9시에 집에 가요.
엄마, 두 시에 학교 앞에서 민수 씨를 만나요. 여덟 시 아니고 아홉 시에 집에 가요.

badAnswers.text: 엄마, 영화관 앞에서 만나요. 여덟 시에 집에 가요.
badAnswers.why: Keeps the wrong place and the wrong time.
No place or time at all.

badAnswers.text: 두 시에 집에 가요. 아홉 시에 학교 앞에서 만나요.
badAnswers.why: The times are swapped between the two plans.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentences are natural and the details are really consistent with the chat.
hints: List the three details first: where they meet, when they meet, when she goes home.
Copy each detail from 민수's messages and keep each time with its own plan, then add polite endings (-요).

rubric.full: Picks a wrong line and can say both wrong details
rubric.none: Picks a line that matches the chat

rubric.full: Place and both times are correct and polite

alternatives: Writing times as numerals (2시, 9시) is fine.
A learner may pick line 5 first or line 2 first; both are wrong lines.
hardCases: Line 4 says 같이 (together); the chat says 'we eat dinner' so this is acceptable.
'오후 두 시' versus 'two o'clock' is the same time here.

cautions.language: Beginner Korean only (해요체, basic particles, numbers up to the thousands). English glosses are given for the few harder words.
cautions.culture: Telling parents your plans is common for younger people in many families; the task only uses it as a reason to be accurate.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or sound. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Choice of the kind of change
Place, times and polite ending in the rewritten note
human: Naturalness and consistency of the rewritten note

subject: korean
title: An invitation with gaps
goal: Decide which facts are missing from a short invitation, notice that a vague answer is still not enough, and ask for what you need.
thinking: Vague answers that look like answers
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to accept or refuse an invitation. Here you first check whether you have enough facts to accept at all.
prerequisites: Knows basic question words (몇 시, 어디)
Can say 'I will go' and 'thank you' in simple polite Korean (갈게요, 고마워요), glossed in the hints
material:
Last week you met 지호 in a language class. Today he sent you a message. You have never been to his home.

지호: 토요일에 우리 집에서 파티를 해요. 꼭 오세요!

(꼭 = please be sure to.)

steps.prompt: You want to go. Which questions must you ask before you can actually get to the party? Choose all that you really need.

options.reveals: How many guests come does not change whether you can find the place or arrive on time.
Useful and polite to ask, but you can arrive without knowing it. It is not needed to get there.
Knowing the occasion may help you choose a gift, but it does not tell you when or where to go.

acceptable.reason: Asking what to bring is considerate and fine. It is just not needed to arrive at the right place and time.

steps.explain: The message gives the day (토요일) but no time, and 우리 집 does not tell you the address of someone you have never visited. Time and place are the two facts you need to arrive.
hints: Imagine it is Saturday morning and you want to leave. What would stop you from leaving?
Sort the questions: which ones help you arrive, and which ones are only nice to know?

steps.prompt: 지호 answers your questions with only one line: '저녁에 오세요.' Do you now know enough about the time?

options.text: Yes. 저녁 is a time, so I can come at any point in the evening.
options.reveals: 저녁 (evening) covers several hours. If you arrive late, you may miss the start; if you arrive early, nobody may be ready.

options.text: Not yet. 저녁 covers several hours, so I still need the exact hour.
Yes. I know the day and the part of the day, so I can plan my arrival.
options.reveals: A day and a part of the day are still not an exact time of arrival.

options.text: Not yet. 저녁 means 'dinner', so I should ask whether food is served.
options.reveals: 저녁 can mean 'evening' or 'dinner'. Here it is a time word because of 에 and 오세요, and food would not tell you when to arrive.

steps.explain: 저녁 only names a part of the day. To arrive at the right moment you still need the hour, for example 여섯 시.
hints: Think about how many hours the word 저녁 can cover.
Ask yourself: could two guests read this sentence and arrive three hours apart?

steps.prompt: Reply to 지호 in polite Korean.

checks.label: asks about the time (몇 시, 언제 ...)
asks about the place (어디, 주소, 장소 ...)
polite ending
no casual question ending (야? / 니?)
says yes / thanks (갈게요, 고마워요, 고맙습니다, 감사 ...)

selfAssess: Did I ask about BOTH time and place?
Is my reply polite enough for someone I met only last week?

modelAnswers.text: 초대해 줘서 고마워요. 몇 시에 시작해요? 집 주소도 알려 주세요.
네, 갈게요! 파티는 몇 시예요? 집이 어디예요?
고맙습니다. 몇 시에 가면 됩니까? 어디입니까?
네 좋아요. 시간과 장소를 알려 주세요.

badAnswers.why: Agrees but asks nothing, so the missing facts stay missing.
Casual endings to someone you hardly know, and no thanks or yes.
No clear yes or thanks, and the ending is abrupt for a new acquaintance.

steps.humanReview: Whether the tone suits a new acquaintance and the questions are clear.
hints: Start by thanking him or saying you will come (고마워요 = thank you, 갈게요 = I will go).
Which facts from your earlier question list does a person need before leaving home? Ask for them with a polite ending (-요).

rubric.full: Picks time and place and leaves out the nice-to-know questions
rubric.partial: Picks only one of time and place, or adds only the considerate question
rubric.none: Picks questions that do not help you arrive

rubric.full: Says yes politely and asks for both time and place
rubric.partial: Asks about only one of them or is not polite

alternatives: Asking what to bring in addition to time and place is accepted.
A learner may think 'my friend will pick me up' makes the address unnecessary; ask for such an assumption to be written.
hardCases: If 지호 had told you the address in an earlier chat, the place question would not be needed; the material says you have never been there.

cautions.language: Beginner Korean only (해요체, basic particles, numbers up to the thousands). English glosses are given for the few harder words.
cautions.culture: Bringing a small gift to a home party is common but not required; the task does not test it.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or sound. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Time and place questions and polite ending in the reply

subject: korean
title: A basket with rules
goal: Read several conditions in a short shopping chat, then build more than one basket that meets all of them and report one basket in Korean.
thinking: Checking an example against all conditions
Seeing that limits allow many answers
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to say prices. Here you use numbers, comparison and 'at least' and 'not more than' together to find baskets that fit.
prerequisites: Knows numbers up to thousands (천, 오백)
material:
민지: 오늘 시장에서 과일을 사요. 사과는 한 개에 천 원, 귤은 한 개에 오백 원이에요.
민지: 사과도 사고 귤도 사요. 그런데 사과가 귤보다 적어요.
민지: 과일은 모두 일곱 개 이상 사요. 오천 원을 넘으면 안 돼요.

(이상 = this number or more. 넘으면 안 돼요 = must not go over. -보다 = than.)

steps.prompt: In 민지's second message, what does '사과가 귤보다 적어요' tell you about the basket?

options.text: There are more apples than tangerines.
options.reveals: 적어요 means 'few / less'. -보다 marks the thing you compare with, so the apples are the smaller number.

options.text: There are as many apples as tangerines.
options.reveals: The sentence compares two amounts and says one is smaller; it does not say they are equal.

options.text: There are fewer apples than tangerines.
There are no apples in the basket.
options.reveals: The line before says 사과도 사고, so apples are in the basket; 적어요 says 'fewer', not 'none'.

steps.explain: A (사과가) B (귤보다) 적어요 = A is fewer than B. So the number of apples is smaller than the number of tangerines.
hints: Find which fruit is the subject (marked with 가) and which fruit is the thing compared with (marked with 보다).
Read 적어요 as 'is a small amount' and decide which fruit has the smaller amount.

steps.prompt: Someone suggests 3 apples and 5 tangerines. Which of 민지's conditions does this basket break?

options.reveals: 3 apples are fewer than 5 tangerines, so this condition is fine.
3 + 5 = 8 pieces of fruit, which is 7 or more, so this is fine.
The basket has both apples and tangerines, so this is fine.

steps.explain: 3 apples cost 3,000 won and 5 tangerines cost 2,500 won, together 5,500 won. That is over 5,000. The other three conditions are met.
hints: Check the conditions one at a time with the numbers 3 and 5.
For the money condition, work out the price of the apples and of the tangerines separately, then add.

steps.prompt: Find 3 different baskets that satisfy EVERY condition in 민지's messages. a = number of apples (사과), t = number of tangerines (귤).

constraints.fail: Buy whole pieces of fruit only (a whole number of 개).
사과도 사고 귤도 사요: at least one of each.
사과가 귤보다 적어요: apples must be fewer than tangerines.
일곱 개 이상: at least 7 pieces of fruit in total.
The total is over 5,000 won (apple 1,000 each, tangerine 500 each).

steps.explain: For example 1 apple + 7 tangerines = 4,500 won; 2 + 5 = 4,500 won; 3 + 4 = 5,000 won. Many baskets fit because the messages give limits, not one exact order.
hints: Put the conditions into your own words first: fewer apples than tangerines, at least 7 pieces, at most 5,000 won.
Try 1 apple and find a number of tangerines that makes at least 7 pieces; then check the price.
Check the money last: 1,000 x apples + 500 x tangerines, then change the number of apples.

because.prompt: Pick ONE of your baskets and tell 민지 in a short polite message how many apples and tangerines you will buy and the total price.

checks.label: polite ending
gives the apple count
gives the tangerine count
says the total in won (원)

selfAssess: Do the numbers in my message match one basket I built?
Is the total right (1,000 x apples + 500 x tangerines)?

modelAnswers.text: 사과는 한 개, 귤은 일곱 개 살게요. 4,500원이에요.

because.humanReview: Whether the counts and the total in the message really belong to one valid basket.
hints: Take one basket from the list above and write down its two numbers.
Say the apples, then the tangerines, then the total in won.

rubric.full: Understands the comparison and checks the price condition correctly
rubric.none: Reverses the comparison and miscounts the price

rubric.full: Three different valid baskets and a correct report in Korean
rubric.partial: Valid baskets but a report with wrong numbers

alternatives: Exactly 5,000 won is allowed because the message says it must not go over 5,000.
Other baskets also work: for example 1 apple + 8 tangerines, 2 + 6.
hardCases: A learner may read '일곱 개 이상' as 'more than seven'. The task counts 7 as allowed.

cautions.language: Beginner Korean only (해요체, basic particles, numbers up to the thousands). English glosses are given for the few harder words.
cautions.culture: Prices and market habits vary; the prices here are invented.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or sound. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Checking every basket against all conditions
Counts, total and polite ending in the report

subject: korean
title: Who did it? The sentence doesn't say
goal: Follow a short chat that leaves out subjects, notice how your reading of who did what changes, and rewrite a sentence so that nobody can misread it.
thinking: Revising a reading as information arrives
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to fill in 이/가 or 은/는. Here you see why a missing subject can mislead and how to repair the sentence.
material: 하나 talks with her friend 준호 about last weekend. In Korean the subject is often left out when it seems clear. Read slowly: the story comes in three parts.

steps.prompt: Read each part, choose the reading that seems most likely, then continue. Your answer may change as you read more.
hints: Decide using only what you have read so far.
Look at which words name a person and which verbs have no person attached to them.

stages.info: 하나: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 비빔밥을 만들었어요.

options.reveals: The sentence says 만들었어요, so someone did it, but the only people in the story are 하나 and her younger sibling.

stages.after: The second sentence has no subject. Korean often leaves out a subject that is clear from the context, but here the sibling (동생이) is the last person named and 하나 is the speaker, so at this point you cannot be sure.

stages.info:
준호: 동생이 요리를 잘해요?
하나: 아니요. 동생은 요리를 못해요.
stages.ask: Who most likely made the bibimbap now?

options.reveals: 하나 says her sibling cannot cook, so this is unlikely, but she has not said who cooked yet.
The first part says 만들었어요 (made), so someone cooked it.
Her answer is about the sibling's skill. It does not say that she shared the cooking.

stages.after: 하나 probably made it herself, but she answered a question about her sibling's skill, so it is still only a likely reading.

stages.info: 하나: 그래서 제가 만들었어요. 맛있게 먹었어요. 설거지는 동생이 했어요.

options.reveals: 하나 is the one who said 제가 만들었어요; nothing marks the sibling alone as the one who ate. 설거지는 동생이 has a marker, but 먹었어요 does not.
맛있게 먹었어요 says that it was eaten and enjoyed.

stages.after: 먹었어요 again has no subject. It is most naturally 하나, maybe with her sibling. When a person is clearly marked (동생이 했어요), the marker tells you who; when nothing is marked, you must use context and sometimes ask.

steps.reflect: Korean often drops the subject when context supplies it, but the last person you read about is not always the one doing the next action. Look for markers (이/가, 은/는, 제가) and keep the reading open when nothing is marked. If it matters, ask.

steps.prompt: Rewrite 하나's first two sentences in polite Korean so that nobody can misread who made the bibimbap: it was 하나 herself, as you learned in the chat. Original: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 비빔밥을 만들었어요.

checks.label: says that 하나 herself made / cooked it, in the past (제가 만들었 / 제가 요리했 ...)
does not say that the sibling made it
polite ending

selfAssess: Can a reader tell who made the bibimbap without looking at the chat?
Did I still say that the sibling came to my home?

modelAnswers.text: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 제가 비빔밥을 만들었어요.
어제 동생이 왔어요. 비빔밥은 동생이 아니라 제가 만들었어요.
modelAnswers.note: Names the person who did NOT make it as well.

modelAnswers.text: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 제가 요리했어요.
어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 제가 만들었어요.

badAnswers.text: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 비빔밥을 만들었어요.
badAnswers.why: Same as the original: no one is named for 만들었어요.
Does not say who made it.

badAnswers.text: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 동생이 비빔밥을 만들었어요.
badAnswers.why: Names the wrong person: the chat says the sibling cannot cook and 하나 made it.

badAnswers.text: 어제 동생이 우리 집에 왔어요. 제가 비빔밥을 만들어요.
badAnswers.why: Present tense, but the cooking already happened.

steps.humanReview: Whether the new sentence is natural and really removes the ambiguity.
hints: Compare your sentence with the original: which information is missing for the second sentence?
A particle after a person word (-가 / -이) shows that this person did the action.

rubric.full: Keeps more than one reading open at first and moves to the best one as clues appear
rubric.partial: Commits too early but corrects later
rubric.none: Picks a reading that the text contradicts

rubric.full: Names the doer clearly in polite Korean
rubric.partial: Names the doer but with wrong particle or no polite ending

alternatives: '하나 and her sibling together' is a fair reading at stage 1.
Different wording such as '제가 요리했어요' is fine if it names the person (the automatic check only looks for 만들).
hardCases: The chat never says who ate in stage 3 with a marker, so two readings stay possible.

cautions.language: Beginner Korean only (해요체, basic particles, numbers up to the thousands). English glosses are given for the few harder words.
cautions.culture: Home cooking and visiting siblings are everyday topics; no cultural background is needed.
cautions.accessibility: All material is text; nothing depends on colour or sound. Romanization is not provided.

auto: Stage choices are compared with a set of reasonable readings
비빔밥, a named doer before 만들, polite ending in the rewrite
human: Whether the learner still sees the second reading afterwards
